questions.q: The λ-closure of a state can be the empty set if that state has no outgoing λ-transitions.
questions.explain: A λ-closure always contains the state itself, so it is never empty. A state with no λ-arrows has the closure {q}. For example, λ-closure(11) = {11}.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has the λ-transitions 1→2, 1→8, 2→3, 2→5 and 8→9, and no other λ-transitions leave these states. What is λ-closure(1)?
questions.explain: Include 1 itself, then follow λ-arrows transitively: 1→2→3, 1→2→5, 1→8→9. That gives {1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9}.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has the λ-transitions 7→2, 7→8, 2→3, 2→5 and 8→9. States 3, 5 and 9 have no λ-transitions. Which states are in λ-closure(7)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(7) contains 7 itself plus everything reachable using only λ-arrows: 2 and 8 directly, then 3 and 5 through 2, and 9 through 8. So it is {2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9}.

questions.q: For a set of states X, how is λ-closure(X) defined?
choices: The union of λ-closure(q) over every q in X
The intersection of λ-closure(q) over every q in X
The λ-closure of the smallest-numbered state in X
The set X itself, since closures apply only to single states
questions.explain: The closure of a set is the union of the closures of its members. The textbook left this out, but the definition of the input transition function needs it.

questions.q: λ-closure(∅) = ∅.
questions.explain: With no members there is nothing to take closures of, so the result is the empty set. This case matters because δ(q, a) is often empty.

questions.q: Why does the definition of the input transition function t need the λ-closure of a set of states, not just of a single state?
choices: Because δ(q, a) in an NFA-λ returns a set of states
Because the DFA's start state is always the set Q
Because λ-transitions can only leave final states
Because t must return exactly one state per symbol
questions.explain: In an NFA-λ, δ(q_j, a) is a set of states that may be empty. The definition takes λ-closure(δ(q_j, a)), so it needs the closure of a set.

questions.q: Which expression defines the input transition function t(q_i, a) of an NFA-λ with transition function δ?
choices: Union over q_j in λ-closure(q_i) of λ-closure(δ(q_j, a))
Union over q_j in λ-closure(q_i) of δ(q_j, a)
λ-closure(δ(q_i, a)), using only q_i itself
Sum over q_j in λ-closure(q_i) of |δ(q_j, a)|
questions.explain: Take λ-moves first (every q_j in λ-closure(q_i)), take one a-step from each, take λ-moves after (the closure of where you land), and union everything. The big symbol is set union, not summation.

questions.q: An NFA-λ over {a, b} has states Q0 (start), Q1 (final) and Q2, with transitions Q0 –a→ Q0, Q0 –a→ Q1, Q0 –a→ Q2, Q1 –b→ Q1 and Q2 –λ→ Q1. What is t(Q2, b)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(Q2) = {Q1, Q2}. Q2 has no b-arrow, but Q1 goes to Q1 on b, and λ-closure(Q1) = {Q1}. Answering ∅ means you forgot the closure before the step.

questions.q: An NFA-λ over {a, b} has states Q0 (start), Q1 (final) and Q2, with transitions Q0 –a→ Q0, Q0 –a→ Q1, Q0 –a→ Q2, Q1 –b→ Q1 and Q2 –λ→ Q1. What is t(Q2, a)?
questions.explain: λ-closure(Q2) = {Q1, Q2}, and neither Q1 nor Q2 has an a-arrow. No state in the closure can step on a, so t(Q2, a) = ∅.

questions.q: In an NFA-λ, λ-closure(4) = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}. Among these states, the only symbol arrows are 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6 and 9 –b→ 10. What is t(4, a)?
questions.explain: Go through the closure of 4: only 3 can step on a, and it lands on 4. Then take λ-closure(4) = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}. Writing {4} forgets the closure after the step.

questions.q: In an NFA-λ, λ-closure(4) = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}. Among these states, the only symbol arrows are 3 –a→ 4, 5 –b→ 6 and 9 –b→ 10. Also λ-closure(6) = {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} and λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}. What is t(4, b)?
questions.explain: Two members of the closure step on b: 5 goes to 6 and 9 goes to 10. Union their closures: {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9} ∪ {10, 11}.

questions.q: In an NFA-λ, λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}. State 10 has no a-arrow, 11 –a→ 12, and state 12 has no λ-transitions. What is t(10, a)?
questions.explain: 11 is in the closure of 10 and steps to 12 on a. λ-closure(12) = {12}, so t(10, a) = {12}.

questions.q: If no state in λ-closure(q) has an arrow on symbol a, then t(q, a) = ∅.
questions.explain: Every δ(q_j, a) is empty, their closures are empty, and a union of empty sets is ∅ (A ∪ ∅ = A).

questions.q: State 9 has no λ-transitions, 9 –b→ 10, and λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}. A student writes t(9, b) = {10}. What did the student forget?
choices: The λ-closure after taking the b-step
The λ-closure before taking the b-step
Including state 9 itself in the answer
Unioning in the trap state ∅
questions.explain: After the step lands on 10, you take λ-closure(10) = {10, 11}. The correct value is t(9, b) = {10, 11}. Copy the closure from your closure table instead of working it out again.

questions.q: In the subset construction from an NFA-λ with start state q0, which set does the DFA's start state correspond to?
choices: λ-closure(q0)
The set of all NFA-λ final states
t(q0, a) for the first symbol a
questions.explain: The DFA starts in λ-closure(q0), since the NFA-λ can reach every state in it from q0 before reading any input.

questions.q: If an NFA-λ has start state Q0 and λ-closure(Q0) = {Q0, Q1}, then the DFA built from it starts in the state {Q0}.
questions.explain: The DFA start state is λ-closure(Q0) = {Q0, Q1}, not {Q0}. Using {q0} is a common mistake.

questions.q: A DFA state X (a set of NFA-λ states) is being processed. Where does its arrow on symbol a go?
choices: To the state for the union of t(q, a) over all q in X
To the state for the intersection of t(q, a) over q in X
To the state for t(q, a), where q is any one member of X
To the state for λ-closure(X), skipping the symbol a
questions.explain: Look at the rows of the t table for the states in X and the column for a, then union those entries. Reuse an existing DFA state if that set already has one.

questions.q: An NFA-λ over {a, b} has this input transition table: t(Q0,a) = {Q0, Q1, Q2}, t(Q0,b) = ∅, t(Q1,a) = ∅, t(Q1,b) = {Q1}, t(Q2,a) = ∅, t(Q2,b) = {Q1}. In the DFA, where does the b-arrow from state {Q0, Q1, Q2} go?
questions.explain: Union the b-column entries for rows Q0, Q1 and Q2: ∅ ∪ {Q1} ∪ {Q1} = {Q1}.

questions.q: An NFA-λ over {a, b} has λ-closure(Q0) = {Q0} and this input transition table: t(Q0,a) = {Q0, Q1, Q2}, t(Q0,b) = ∅, t(Q1,a) = ∅, t(Q1,b) = {Q1}, t(Q2,a) = ∅, t(Q2,b) = {Q1}. How many states does the DFA from the subset construction have, counting the trap state?
questions.explain: Start at {Q0}. On a it goes to {Q0, Q1, Q2} (new) and on b to ∅ (new, the trap). {Q0, Q1, Q2} loops to itself on a and goes to {Q1} (new) on b. {Q1} goes to ∅ on a and to itself on b. That gives {Q0}, ∅, {Q0, Q1, Q2} and {Q1}.

questions.q: If the union for a DFA state and a symbol gives a set that already has a DFA state, you still create a new state for it.
questions.explain: You draw the arrow to the existing state for that set. You create a new state only for a set that doesn't have one yet.

questions.q: Several DFA states are still missing outgoing arrows. Which one should the subset construction process next?
choices: Any of them; the order does not matter
The one with the most NFA-λ states in it
The one that was created first, always
The one containing a final state of the NFA-λ
questions.explain: You can pick any unfinished state. You keep going until every DFA state has one outgoing arrow per symbol.

questions.q: In an NFA-λ over {a, b}: t(q, a) = {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9} for q in {2, 3, 6, 7}; t(q, a) = ∅ for q in {5, 8, 9}; t(q, a) = {12} for q in {10, 11}. In the DFA, where does the a-arrow from the state {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11} go?
questions.explain: Union the a-entries for every member: {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9} from 2, 3, 6 and 7, nothing from 5, 8 and 9, and {12} from 10 and 11. The result is {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12}.

questions.q: {Q0, Q1, Q3} and {Q0, Q3, Q1} are two different DFA states.
questions.explain: DFA states are sets, and order inside a set doesn't matter, so these are the same state.

questions.q: In the subset construction, which DFA states are final?
choices: Those whose set contains at least one NFA-λ final state
Those whose set contains only NFA-λ final states
Those reached by strings the language should accept
Only the state whose set equals λ-closure(q0)
questions.explain: A DFA state is final if and only if its set contains at least one final state of the NFA-λ. Apply the rule directly. Trying to work out which strings should be accepted can take forever.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has Q1 as its only final state. The subset construction gives the DFA states {Q0}, ∅, {Q0, Q1, Q2} and {Q1}. Which DFA states are final?
questions.explain: Only the sets containing Q1 are final: {Q0, Q1, Q2} and {Q1}. If you skip this step, the DFA accepts nothing.

questions.q: If every state of a DFA built by the subset construction is final except the trap state, the DFA accepts every string.
questions.explain: The trap state (∅) is never final, so any string that reaches it is rejected.

questions.q: When is the DFA's start state final?
choices: Exactly when the NFA-λ accepts the empty string λ
Exactly when q0 has at least one λ-transition
Only when the NFA-λ has a single final state
Never; start states are not final in this method
questions.explain: The start state is λ-closure(q0). It contains a final state exactly when the NFA-λ can reach a final state without reading input, which means it accepts λ.

questions.q: During the subset construction, the union for some DFA state on symbol b comes out to ∅. What do you draw?
choices: An arrow on b to a trap state for ∅, which loops to itself on every symbol
Nothing; the b-transition from that state is simply left out
An arrow on b back to the same state, as a self-loop
An arrow on b to the start state, λ-closure(q0)
questions.explain: ∅ is the trap state, which is also rejecting. Create it if it doesn't exist yet, and give it a self-loop on every symbol.

questions.q: The trap state ∅ produced by the subset construction is never a final state.
questions.explain: ∅ contains no NFA-λ states, so it can't contain a final one. It also loops to itself, so strings that reach it are rejected.

questions.q: In a DFA, every state must have exactly one outgoing arrow for every symbol, so a machine with a missing transition is not a DFA.
questions.explain: That is why you draw the trap state with its self-loops instead of leaving transitions out.

questions.q: JFLAP's Convert to DFA result shows no trap state. How does JFLAP treat the missing transitions?
choices: They implicitly go to a rejecting trap state
They implicitly loop back to the current state
They make JFLAP label the machine an NFA
They implicitly go to the start state
questions.explain: JFLAP sends missing transitions to an undrawn trap state and still calls the machine a DFA. It calls a machine an NFA only if some state has two arrows on the same symbol, or a λ-arrow. On paper, draw the trap state yourself.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has 4 states. What is the maximum number of states the DFA from the subset construction can have, counting the trap state?
questions.explain: Each DFA state is a subset of Q, including ∅. There are 2^4 = 16 subsets.

questions.q: An NFA-λ has 12 states. What is the maximum number of states the DFA from the subset construction can have, counting the trap state?
questions.explain: 2^12 = 4096, the number of subsets of a 12-element set.

questions.q: Why is 4! = 24 the wrong bound on the number of DFA states built from a 4-state NFA-λ?
choices: DFA states are unordered sets, so you count subsets, not orderings
4! is too small, since a state can appear several times in a set
Factorials count subsets, and the trap state must be added to it
The real bound is n + 1, since only one trap state can be added
questions.explain: A factorial counts permutations, or orderings. DFA states are sets, where order doesn't matter, so the bound is the number of subsets: 2^4 = 16. n + 1 is only what happens in easy cases.

questions.q: The maximum number of DFA states equals the cardinality of which set built from the NFA-λ's state set Q? (Two words.)
questions.explain: The power set P(Q) is the set of all subsets of Q. Its size is 2^|Q|.

questions.q: The subset construction always terminates, because every DFA state is a subset of the NFA-λ's finite state set Q.
questions.explain: Only finitely many subsets exist (2^|Q|), so the construction eventually runs out of new sets to create.

questions.q: In practice the DFA usually has far fewer than 2^n states, because the t-table entries repeat and their unions keep producing sets that already exist.
questions.explain: For example, the 12-state machine from class (bound 4096) gives a DFA with only 4 states.
